questions.question: Your AI roster fills Sunday PM with "Tom (relief)". Your note says Tom hasn't confirmed Sunday PM, and Ben can't milk on his own. What do you do?

answers.text: Leave it in, because Tom will probably say yes by Friday anyway.
answers.feedback: A probable yes is still a guess. If Tom can't come, the roster on the wall says the milking is covered when it isn't.

answers.text: Change Sunday PM to UNCOVERED and note Tom hasn't confirmed.
answers.feedback: Right. The gap stays visible until Tom confirms or you arrange cover yourself.

answers.text: Put Ben on by himself, since it's only one milking on a Sunday.
answers.feedback: That breaks your own pairing rule. The rule exists because Ben is still learning, and Sunday afternoon is no different.

answers.text: Ask the AI to find someone else and accept whoever it picks.
answers.feedback: Everyone else is off or unavailable, so any name the AI picks breaks your note. Arranging cover is your job.

questions.feedback: An AI roster should show a gap as a gap. Unconfirmed shifts stay marked until a person confirms them.

questions.question: Priya can't do Thursday PM because of a physio appointment. What goes in your roster prompt?

answers.text: Priya: not available Thursday PM.
answers.feedback: Right. That's all the AI needs to build the roster. The reason is Priya's business.

answers.text: Priya: physio Thursday PM, so keep her week light.
answers.feedback: The health detail adds nothing the AI needs, and asking it to go easy on her hands a judgement about her health to a chatbot.

answers.text: Priya: off Thursday PM for physio on her knee.
answers.feedback: Same constraint, more private detail. Free tools may keep what you type, and her medical appointment doesn't belong there.

answers.text: Leave her out and fix Thursday PM by hand later.
answers.feedback: Leave the constraint out and the AI will probably roster her on Thursday PM. Give it the rule and keep the reason.

questions.feedback: Give the AI the rule, not the reason. Staff health and personal details stay out of AI chats and group chats.

questions.question: You've asked the AI to translate the roster message for a team member who reads more easily in Tagalog. How should you use the translation?

answers.text: Send only the translation, since that's the version he'll read.
answers.feedback: If the translation has a mistake, there's no checked version to compare it with. Keep the English roster as the master.

answers.text: Keep the English roster as master and get a bilingual workmate to check it.
answers.feedback: Right. The checked English roster stays on the wall, and a person who reads both languages catches what the AI got wrong.

answers.text: Have the AI translate it back to English and compare the two yourself.
answers.feedback: Back-translation can catch big slips, but the same tool can repeat its own mistake. A bilingual person is a better check.

answers.text: Post it straight away, since roster translations are usually accurate.
answers.feedback: Usually accurate isn't checked. Days and times are exactly the details a bad translation scrambles.

questions.feedback: A translation is a copy of the checked roster, not a replacement. Have someone who reads both languages check it.

questions.question: Select ALL that apply: Your notes give a spray window of 13 to 15 October and no product name. Which lines in the AI's neighbour notice must you fix before it goes out?

answers.text: Spraying will start at 7 am on Tuesday 13 October.
answers.feedback: Fix it. The day and time are invented. Your notes give a three-day window and no start time.

answers.text: The herbicide is safe for people, pets and stock.
answers.feedback: Fix it. Nobody has checked that, and a notice should never promise safety. Any label advice comes through the contractor.

answers.text: Please tell us about any beehives near the boundary.
answers.feedback: This one can stay. It asks for information that helps you and the contractor plan, and promises nothing.

answers.text: It will be applied at 2 litres per hectare.
answers.feedback: Fix it. You never gave a rate. Remove it, and leave product details to the contractor as [confirm: …].

answers.text: Any questions, call Sam on the farm mobile.
answers.feedback: This came from your notes, so it can stay once the number is filled in.

questions.feedback: Anything in a notice that you didn't supply, such as a time, a rate or a safety claim, is a guess. Mark it [confirm: …] or delete it.

questions.question: Your AI spray notice reads well, and the neighbours expect it today. The product and start time still say [confirm: …]. What happens next?

answers.text: Send it now as it is, and let the neighbours ring Sam if they want the missing details.
answers.feedback: The neighbours would get a notice with blanks in it and still not know the product or time. Fill the gaps first.

answers.text: Get the product, time and label advice from the operator, and check regional rules.
answers.feedback: Right. The operator knows what's going in the tank and when. Your regional plan sets who needs the notice and how far ahead.

answers.text: Ask the AI which product is normally used on thistles and fill that in for now.
answers.feedback: That swaps a visible gap for a plausible guess. Only the operator knows what product they're using.

answers.text: Delete the [confirm] lines so the notice looks finished, then send it out today.
answers.feedback: Then the neighbours get a notice with no product or start time and no sign that anything is missing.

questions.feedback: AI drafts the wording. The spray operator confirms the product, timing and label, and you check the notice against your regional rules.

questions.question: Six calves have had loose yellow scours for two days and are still drinking. The AI's email to your vet says: "We have a likely rotavirus outbreak and have started electrolytes twice daily." You haven't started anything. What do you do?

answers.text: Rewrite it to describe what you've seen and ask what the vet needs.
answers.feedback: Right. The vet works from your observations. The cause and the treatment are the vet's call.

answers.text: Keep the rotavirus line, because it gives the vet a useful head start.
answers.feedback: It's the AI's guess written as your finding, and it can steer the vet before anyone has looked at the calves.

answers.text: Keep it all, but add a note saying the AI suggested the diagnosis.
answers.feedback: Labelling the guess doesn't fix it, and the treatment line is still false because you haven't started anything.

answers.text: Send it now, and ring the vet later if the calves get any worse.
answers.feedback: The email describes a treatment you never gave, so fix it first. And if calves go down or stop drinking, ring straight away.

questions.feedback: Emails to the vet describe what you saw. Leave diagnosis and treatment to the vet, and phone for anything urgent.

questions.question: Thursday's notebook says "vat 2 seal leaking - Sam to swap Sat". The AI log for Thursday says "Vat 2 seal replaced." What should the log say?

answers.text: Done, because Sam is reliable and it will be swapped by Saturday.
answers.feedback: It hadn't happened on Thursday. If Saturday slips, the log says a leaking seal was fixed.

answers.text: Planned for Saturday, with Sam's name, and marked done after the swap.
answers.feedback: Right. The log matches the note, and it gets updated when the job actually happens.

answers.text: Leave the seal out of the log entirely until the swap is done.
answers.feedback: Then the leak isn't recorded at all, and nobody can follow up if Saturday slips.

answers.text: Not confirmed, because nobody has had a proper look at the seal.
answers.feedback: Someone saw it leaking, and the swap has a person and a day. Planned is the accurate status.

questions.feedback: Planned never becomes done in a summary. A job is done when the record says it happened.

questions.question: Select ALL that apply: Which of these are sound uses of AI with farm records?

answers.text: Tidying a shed notebook page into a log with a "not yet confirmed" list.
answers.feedback: Sound. The log is easier to read, the open items are visible, and the original page stays with it.

answers.text: Summarising the week's logs for the owner, then checking each "done" against the source.
answers.feedback: Sound. The summary saves time, and checking each "done" catches anything that drifted.

answers.text: Keeping an AI summary of heifer movements instead of entering them in NAIT.
answers.feedback: Not sound. NAIT movements must be recorded in NAIT within 48 hours. A summary somewhere else doesn't count.

answers.text: Writing "planting maintained" as FEP evidence when the note says the guards need checking.
answers.feedback: Not sound. It turns a job still to do into a claim. FEP evidence is dated photos and records of what happened.

answers.text: Listing visitors from the sign-in sheet for a meeting, and keeping the signed sheet.
answers.feedback: Sound. The list is handy for the meeting, and the signed sheet stays the record.

questions.feedback: AI can tidy and summarise records. It can't replace the record itself or upgrade a plan into a fact.
